wonders.title: Forenoon & Overmorrow
wonders.subtitle: Lost Words for Lost Time
wonders.fact: English used to have precise words for every slice of the day. Forenoon is the specific period between morning and solar noon. Overmorrow means the day after tomorrow, and ereyesterday is the day before yesterday. Crepuscular refers to the twilight hours just before sunrise or after sunset—when cats and deer are most active. We've lost these beautiful, specific time words in modern English, replacing precision with vagueness.
wonders.funFact: Animals like cats are 'crepuscular'—they're most active during twilight, not at night!
wonders.visualDescription: A beautiful gradient from dawn to dusk showing the different periods of the day with subtle light changes

wonders.title: Mondegreens
wonders.subtitle: Why You Sing the Wrong Lyrics
wonders.fact: A mondegreen happens when your brain misinterprets a stream of sound and fills in gaps with familiar words. The term was coined in 1954 by writer Sylvia Wright, who misheard the Scottish ballad line 'and laid him on the green' as 'and Lady Mondegreen.' Your brain isn't being silly—it's doing something incredibly sophisticated: pattern matching. When uncertain, it predicts the most likely sound based on your vocabulary and context.
wonders.funFact: Famously, people mishear 'Blinded by the Light' as 'Wrapped up like a deuce'—for decades!
wonders.visualDescription: Split screen showing what someone hears vs. what was actually said, with sound waves visualized

wonders.title: Eye Floaters
wonders.subtitle: Cellular Shadows on Your Retina
wonders.fact: Those squiggly, translucent worms drifting across your vision are called muscae volitantes (Latin: 'flying flies'). They aren't on your eye's surface—they're tiny clumps of protein or blood cells floating inside the vitreous humor (the gel-like substance filling your eyeball). You're not seeing the floaters themselves; you're seeing the shadows they cast directly onto your retina. This is why they're always where you're looking—they move with your eyes.
wonders.funFact: About 7 in 10 people experience floaters—they're completely normal and harmless!
wonders.visualDescription: A close-up view of the human eye with tiny shadows floating inside the vitreous humor, with light rays shown

wonders.title: Blue Field Entoptic Phenomenon
wonders.subtitle: Seeing Your Own White Blood Cells
wonders.fact: Look closely at a bright blue sky and you might see tiny bright dots darting around in squiggly paths. You're literally watching your own white blood cells moving through the capillaries in front of your retina! White blood cells transmit blue light better than red blood cells, so your brain perceives them as moving pinpricks of bright light. This phenomenon is so pervasive that every human has likely experienced it, yet most don't know what they're seeing.
wonders.funFact: This is literally your immune system in action—you're watching cells that protect you from disease!
wonders.visualDescription: Animated view of white blood cells flowing through blood vessels with blue light passing through

wonders.title: Petrichor
wonders.subtitle: The Smell of Rain on Earth
wonders.fact: That earthy, clean smell when rain hits dry ground is called petrichor. It comes from two sources: geosmin (a compound made by soil bacteria) and plant oils (secreted by plants during dry spells). When raindrops hit the ground, they trap air bubbles underneath. These bubbles shoot upward through the drop, pop, and spray micro-particles into the air, carrying geosmin straight to your nose. Humans are ridiculously sensitive to it: we can detect geosmin at 5 parts per trillion—better than a shark's ability to smell blood.
wonders.funFact: Plants release geosmin to signal rain to animals—it's a natural communication system!
wonders.visualDescription: Raindrops hitting earth with visible aerosol particles being released into the air, showing molecular structure

wonders.title: The Tiny Jeans Pocket
wonders.subtitle: A Relic from the Gold Rush
wonders.fact: That tiny pocket inside your main jeans pocket was designed in 1873 by Levi Strauss for pocket watches. Cowboys and railway workers needed a safe, snug place to store their watches so they wouldn't scratch or drop out while riding horses. Even though pocket watches became obsolete, the pattern was never changed. Today, we still have this vestigial pocket in nearly every pair of jeans—a design relic surviving 150+ years of fashion evolution.
wonders.funFact: Most people today use it for coins, USB drives, or AirPods—yet it still serves a purpose!
wonders.visualDescription: Historical photograph of a cowboy with visible pocket watch next to modern jeans showing the tiny pocket

wonders.title: QWERTY Keyboards
wonders.subtitle: Intentionally Inefficient Design
wonders.fact: The QWERTY layout was invented in 1873 by Christopher Sholes for mechanical typewriters. Early typewriters had metal typebars that swung up to hit paper. If typists typed too fast with keys placed next to each other, the metal arms would collide and jam. Sholes purposefully scattered commonly paired letters (like 'S' and 'T', or 'T' and 'H') far apart to slow down typists slightly, giving the mechanical levers time to fall back into place. This inefficiency was a feature, not a bug.
wonders.funFact: The Dvorak keyboard (1936) is more efficient, yet QWERTY survived through simple inertia!
wonders.visualDescription: Split screen showing mechanical typewriter typebars colliding vs. QWERTY layout spreading letters apart

wonders.title: Pen Cap Hole
wonders.subtitle: A Life-Saving Design Feature
wonders.fact: That small hole at the top of a BIC ballpoint pen cap isn't for keeping ink from drying out—it's a life-saving ventilation feature. People frequently chew on pen caps, making them one of the most commonly swallowed household items. If a cap accidentally gets inhaled and lodges in someone's trachea, the hole ensures an airway remains open so they can breathe until emergency help arrives. This tiny hole has literally saved lives.
wonders.funFact: This regulation was added after several documented choking incidents—good design can save lives!
wonders.visualDescription: Cross-section of a pen cap showing the ventilation hole with airway visualization

wonders.title: Wine Bottle Punt
wonders.subtitle: The Bottom Dent Has Purpose
wonders.fact: That deep indentation at the bottom of a wine bottle is called a punt. Historically, when glassblowers made bottles by hand, the seam at the bottom was pushed inward so the bottle wouldn't wobble or spill on a flat table. Today, it serves an even more important structural purpose: it distributes pressure evenly inside the bottle, which is critical for carbonated drinks like champagne to prevent the bottle from exploding. The punt is functional beauty.
wonders.funFact: Champagne bottles have deeper punts than still wine bottles because they withstand 90+ PSI of pressure!
wonders.visualDescription: Diagram showing how pressure distributes through a wine bottle with and without a punt

wonders.title: Card Shuffles & Universes
wonders.subtitle: 52! Unique Combinations
wonders.fact: Every time you shuffle a standard 52-card deck, the resulting order has likely never existed before in the history of the universe. The total number of ways to arrange 52 cards is 52! (52 factorial)—approximately 8×10^67. To put this in perspective: if every human on Earth shuffled a deck every second since the Big Bang 13.8 billion years ago, we still wouldn't have created all possible combinations. You literally hold infinity in your hands.
wonders.funFact: 52! is a number so large that comparing it to atoms in the universe is almost meaningless!
wonders.visualDescription: Animated visualization of cards shuffling with probability clouds showing the vastness of combinations

wonders.title: Trees Outnumber Stars
wonders.subtitle: Earth's Canopy Is Deeper Than Space
wonders.fact: When we look up at the night sky, space feels infinite. Yet Earth has a surprisingly dense canopy. The Milky Way galaxy contains an estimated 100-400 billion stars. Meanwhile, Earth is home to roughly 3.04 trillion trees. That means there are approximately 8 times more trees on our planet than stars in our home galaxy. Your local forest has more individual trees than humanity can see stars.
wonders.funFact: We discover new tree species every year—the forest is still revealing its secrets!
wonders.visualDescription: Split-screen cosmic perspective: billions of stars on one side, trillions of trees filling the other
